chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Yahya ibn Abdullah ibn Al-Hasan ibn Al-Hasan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ascended the pulpit one day, praised Allah and extolled Him, and sent blessings upon His Prophets (peace be upon them), then said: 'O people! Let the present among you convey to the absent. Indeed, whoever grants respite to an insolvent person, for him with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is a charity equal to his wealth every day until he pays it back in full.'

Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'And if he is in hardship, then respite until he becomes able (to pay). And giving it as charity is better for you if you know that he is insolvent, so give charity on his behalf with your wealth, for that is better for you.'

key_terms.مُعْسِر: Insolvent person (one who cannot pay debt)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for granting respite to an insolvent debtor in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elaborates on the Prophet’s sermon by distinguishing between mere respite and active forgiveness, highlighting the Shia emphasis on benevolent debt management as a form of ongoing charity. This narration underscores the spiritual merit of alleviating financial hardship, a concept deeply rooted in the ethical teachings of the Ahl al-Bayt regarding social justice and economic mercy.
